cells.tense: The structure you keep is holding, and you're inside it rather than pinned under it.
cells.ask: Hand one running piece of it to somebody else this week — a name, a slot, a date — and let their arrangement carry it. What you get back is attention you're not spending on defence.
cells.core:
Some mornings the shape of the day is already there — the thread you keep going, the table of who's doing what, the small machinery under the bigger work. You tend it without announcing it, and the people around you get steadier because the thing you're holding doesn't wobble.

The cost of a setup that works is that it starts to look like it survives on its own. Sort one piece into someone else's hands and leave it there — a slot, a date, a next step. The shape holds; you find out how much of the neatness was ever yours to carry.

cells.tense: You're building the next version in your head before this one has found its floor, so the shape arrives ahead of anyone who'd stand in it.
cells.ask: Before you draft the next plan, go and look at one that's already running and write down where it actually stands — what's done, what's behind, what nobody has touched. A floor under you beats one you're building mid-air.
cells.core:
Your sense of what comes next is strong, and the plan tends to arrive fully formed — you can see the machine before it's switched on, and you're carrying it steady while the room is still reading the brief. That's a real strength, and it's why the thing keeps moving when other things stall.

It just runs ahead of the people who have to live inside it. Instructions get exact, timing gets tight, corrections land before the work does, and the plan stops being something they're part of. Go and put down what's actually there — done, behind, untouched. The plan gets smaller and truer, and the people inside it stop being worked around.

cells.tense: The shape you used to keep has gone quiet, and you're waiting at a door that's already behind you.
cells.ask: Close one thing in the room you're sitting in — a tab, a list, a half-written note — and do one small thing under the new arrangement before you open another. What's left is a corner you can call finished.
cells.core:
There's a rhythm to this when it's going well — certain things on certain days, a standing order to the week, a sense of who's doing what without being asked. You notice it most in the absence: a handover that didn't need explaining, a morning that ran without your hand on it.

What's there now is the bench where the rhythm used to be made. The small open loops are probably still sitting in it — a tab, a list, a message half-replied to — and your attention keeps turning toward them the way it did when they belonged to something live. Pick one and let it end, then do one thing in the space it leaves. The room doesn't fill straight away; the point is that it can.

cells.tense: The pattern is already being set in how you talk to the people around you, and you'd say it set itself.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you decided for the group this week — a rule, a date, a choice about how it works — and say it out loud as a decision rather than an observation. A live thing can be changed; a fact of the room can only be lived with.
cells.core:
You're good at this when you own it — you take a mess and give it a shape the others can stand in, the standing order, the handover, the small rules they work inside without noticing. The work is real, and it's doing what it's meant to do.

You just describe it as though it were the room's own arrangement, something that arranged itself. Any structure is a choice about whom it serves, and this one is serving quietly. Say one choice out loud, in plain words, as something a person made. It stays exactly as good; it stops being something that happens to you.
